title: Bigger or Smaller? Theo’s Big Problem
goal: I can compare and order numbers, and I can find the problem, the try and the fix in a story.

card.desc: You start with a quick review of Week 1. Then you compare 3-digit numbers by lining up the places and starting at the left, use the <, > and = symbols, and put numbers in order, even when the smaller number wins a race. In reading, you follow Theo’s hike to find the conflict, his attempt and the resolution, and link them with cause and effect (Pathways Week 2).

win: You compared, put numbers in order, and found the whole plot. Great work, Ce'Line!

slides.title: Bigger or Smaller? Theo’s Big Problem
slides.text:
Today you learn two big things.
In math, you compare numbers and put them in order.
In reading, Theo’s hike hits a big problem.

notes.do: Before class: 12 blank index cards, a dry-erase board with 2 marker colors, a pencil, and her printed Week 2 Packet (keep it until the end of class). Ce'Line taps and types on the laptop herself today. Sit beside her, not across.
notes.say: Last week you learned what each digit is worth. Today we use that to find which number is bigger. Then we find out what goes wrong on Theo's hike.
notes.listen: 400, or 4 hundreds. If she says 4, point to the hundreds place and ask again: what is a 4 worth when it sits in the hundreds place?

slides.title: Theo’s hike so far
slides.text: Remember Theo’s First Hike from last week?
prompts: Who is the story about? What is he like?
Where is Theo? When does the story happen?
What does Theo want to see at the top?
starters: The story is about … He is …

notes.do: 5 minutes. She answers out loud in full sentences. Praise every detail she remembers by name: "Yes! You remembered the compass."
notes.ask: Who is the story about? Where and when is it? What does Theo want to see at the top?
notes.listen: Theo; brave, careful, a little nervous (his hands were shaky). A hiking trail in the early morning: pine trees, a rocky creek, mist over the valley. He wants to see the whole valley from Lookout Peak, like his grandfather described. If she forgets, tell her: Theo has his father's old brass compass. It matters today.

slides.title: From last week
slides.text: Quick warm-up. Type each answer.

items.q: What is the 7 worth in 374?
items.why: The 7 is in the tens place. It is worth 70.
items.no: Find the place of the 7. Is it ones, tens or hundreds?

items.q: Round 46 to the nearest ten: ____
items.why: 46 is between 40 and 50. The ones digit is 6. 5 or more rounds up: 50.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. Is it 5 or more?

items.q: Round 350 to the nearest hundred.
items.why: Look at the tens digit: 5. 5 or more rounds up. 350 rounds to 400.
no: 300 is rounding down. The tens digit is 5, so round up.
350 is not a hundred. It must be 300 or 400.

items.q: Where and when a story happens is the ____.
items.why: The setting is where and when. Theo’s setting is a hiking trail early in the morning.
items.no: It is a story word from last week. It tells where and when.

notes.do: She types each answer herself. Quick and confident is the goal. Celebrate each right answer.
notes.listen: 70, 50, 400, setting. If she says 7, she named the digit, not its worth: put her finger on the tens place. If she says 300 for 350, ask: is the tens digit 5 or more?

slides.title: Math words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: To look at two numbers and find which is bigger, which is smaller, or if they are the same.
To put numbers in a line, from smallest to biggest or from biggest to smallest.

notes.do: She reads each card out loud, then covers it and says the meaning in her own words.
notes.say: The open side of the symbol always faces the bigger number.
notes.ask: Which word means to put numbers in a line? Which symbol means less than?
notes.listen: Order. The less-than symbol has its point on the left: the first number is smaller.

slides.title: Start with the biggest place
slides.text: Which number is bigger, 463 or 389?

steps.text: Line up the numbers. Hundreds over hundreds.
Look at the hundreds first: 4 and 3.
4 is more than 3. So 463 is bigger. You can stop!
Do not be tricked by the 8 and the 9. The hundreds win first.

slides.tip: Start at the left. The biggest place decides first.

notes.do: Hands-on: she writes 463 and 389 on two index cards and lines them up on the table, hundreds over hundreds. She points to the two hundreds digits.
notes.say: 463 has 4 hundreds. 389 has only 3 hundreds. Even with 8 tens and 9 ones, 389 can't catch up.
notes.ask: Why don't we need to look at the 8 and the 9?
notes.listen: Because 4 hundreds is already more than 3 hundreds. If she says 389 is bigger because 8 and 9 are big digits, draw 4 big squares (hundreds) next to 3 big squares and ask which side has more.

slides.title: A tie? Move to the right.
slides.text: Compare 274 and 281.

steps.text: Hundreds: 2 and 2. A tie! Move one place to the right.
Tens: 7 and 8. 8 is more. So 281 is bigger.
Now try 536 and 532. Hundreds tie. Tens tie, too (3 and 3).
Ones: 6 and 2. 6 is more. So 536 is bigger.
If every place ties, the numbers are equal.

slides.tip: Tie? Move right. Keep going until one digit wins.

notes.do: She makes cards for 274, 281, 536 and 532. For each pair she slides her finger from left to right and says "tie" or "wins" at each place.
notes.listen: The ones place: 6 is more than 2. If she stops at the hundreds and says "they're the same," ask: did EVERY place tie?

slides.title: The symbols
slides.text: We use symbols to show a compare.

steps.text: > means greater than. < means less than.
The open side faces the bigger number. It is like a hungry mouth. It wants the bigger number.
The point faces the smaller number.
389 < 463 reads: 389 is less than 463.
615 = 615 reads: 615 is equal to 615.

slides.tip: Read it left to right, like a sentence.

notes.do: On the whiteboard write 463 ___ 389, then 389 ___ 463. She draws each symbol and reads the whole thing out loud as a sentence.
notes.ask: Which way does the open side face? Why?
notes.listen: Toward 463, the bigger number. She must also READ it: "463 is greater than 389." Saying only "alligator" is not enough; the Pathways retake uses the words greater than and less than.

slides.title: Compare
slides.text: Line up the places. Start at the left.

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 7 is more than 4. So 547 < 574. 547 is less than 574.
items.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.why: Hundreds: 8 is more than 7. So 802 > 799. 802 is greater than 799.
items.no: Start at the left. Look at the hundreds first.
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.why: Every place ties. 615 and 615 are equal: 615 = 615.
items.no: Check each place: hundreds, tens, ones. Is any digit different?
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.q: Which one is true?
items.why: 3 hundreds is less than 6 hundreds. So 362 < 623.
no: The open side must face the bigger number. 623 is bigger.
623 is bigger, so it is not less than 362.
They have the same digits, but in different places. They are not equal.

notes.do: She says each answer as a sentence BEFORE she types: "547 is less than 574."
notes.listen: <, >, =, and 362 < 623. If she types > for 547 ____ 574, she compared the ones (7 and 4). Ask: which place do we look at first? Then, after the hundreds tie, which place comes next?

slides.title: Read the symbols
slides.text: Read each one out loud first.

items.q:
Is this true? 708 > 780
Type true or false.
items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 0 is less than 8. So 708 is less than 780. The sentence is false.
items.no: Hundreds tie. Compare the tens.
items.hint: 0 tens or 8 tens: which is more?

items.q: A sign says 419 < 491. Which number is bigger? Type it.
items.why: The open side faces 491. 491 is bigger.
items.no: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.q: How do you read 256 < 265?
items.why: The point faces 256, so 256 is smaller. Read it: 256 is less than 265.
no: Greater than is >. This symbol is <.
Equal is =. These numbers are not the same.

notes.do: She reads each sentence out loud with the words greater than / less than before answering.
notes.listen: false, 491, less than. If she says true for 708 > 780, cover the ones and compare 70 and 78 first.

slides.title: Put numbers in order
slides.text: Put 524, 342, 435 in order from least to greatest.

steps.text: Least means smallest. Greatest means biggest.
Look at the hundreds: 5, 3, 4.
3 is the smallest. 342 goes first.
Then 4 hundreds: 435. Then 5 hundreds: 524.

slides.tip: Least to greatest: smallest first. Greatest to least: biggest first.

notes.do: Hands-on: she writes the three numbers on index cards, then slides the cards into a line on the table, smallest on the left. On the last step, she points to where each number sits on the number line (342 just past 300, 435 just past 400, 524 just past 500).
notes.ask: Which digit did you look at first? What would greatest to least look like?
notes.listen: The hundreds. Greatest to least is the same cards flipped: 524, 435, 342.

slides.title: Line up the cards
slides.text: Tap the numbers from least to greatest.
slides.why: All four use 4, 9 and 0. Hundreds first: 4 hundreds come before 9 hundreds. Then tens: 0 tens come before 9 tens.
slides.hint: Look at the hundreds digit first. Two numbers start with 4. Which of those two has fewer tens?

notes.do: First she builds it with 4 index cards on the table. Then she taps it on the screen.
notes.ask: 409 and 490 both have 4 hundreds. How did you decide?
notes.listen: "Tie in the hundreds, so I looked at the tens: 0 is less than 9." Same for 904 and 940.

slides.title: When smaller wins
slides.text: In a race, the smallest time is the fastest. Read what wins before you answer!

items.q: Jada ran the trail in 318 seconds. Omar ran it in 381 seconds. Who was faster?
items.why: 318 < 381. Jada’s time is smaller, so Jada was faster.
no: 381 is the bigger time. A bigger time means slower.
318 and 381 are not equal. The tens are different.

items.q: Three hikers carried packs that weigh 264, 246 and 426 ounces. Which pack is the lightest? Type its weight.
items.why: Hundreds: 2, 2, 4. Two packs tie with 2 hundreds. Tens: 4 is less than 6. 246 is the lightest.
items.no: Lightest means smallest. Two numbers have 2 hundreds. Compare their tens.

items.q: Put 732, 723, 327 in order from greatest to least. Type them with commas: ____
items.why: Hundreds: 7, 7, 3. 327 is last. 732 and 723 tie in the hundreds. Tens: 3 is more than 2. So: 732, 723, 327.
items.no: Greatest to least means biggest first.
items.hint: Two numbers have 7 hundreds. Which has more tens?

notes.do: She reads each question out loud and circles the key word on the whiteboard (faster, lightest, greatest) before answering.
notes.ask: In a race, does the bigger number win? Why not?
notes.listen: No. A bigger time means it took longer. Jada, 246, then 732, 723, 327. This is the trap on the Pathways retake: read whether the bigger or the smaller number wins.

slides.title: Math check
slides.text: On your own this time.

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 9 is more than 3. So 693 > 639. 693 is greater than 639.
items.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.q: Which is the smallest: 580, 508, 850? Type it.
items.why: Hundreds: 5, 5, 8. 580 and 508 tie. Tens: 0 is less than 8. 508 is smallest.
items.no: Two numbers have 5 hundreds. Compare their tens.

items.q: Which list goes from least to greatest?
items.why: 417 < 471 < 714 < 741. Smallest first.
no: 471 is bigger than 417. Hundreds tie, then tens: 1 is less than 7.
741 is bigger than 714. It should come last.
That list goes from greatest to least.

notes.do: Hands off. She works alone. Note her FIRST answers on the teacher plan.
notes.listen: 693 > 639, 508, and the first list. All three right on the first try means the math is ready for the Pathways Week 2 Math retake on Monday.

slides.title: Reading words for today
slides.text: Tap each card. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: A problem a character faces in a story.
words.example: Theo’s conflict starts when the trail splits in two.

words.meaning: To find an answer or fix a problem.
words.example: Theo wants to solve his problem on his own.

words.meaning: A try at doing something hard.
words.example: Using a map is a smart attempt to find the way.

words.meaning: How the story’s problem gets fixed by the end.
words.example: In the resolution, the problem is fixed.

words.meaning: What happens (effect) because of something that happened first (cause).
words.example: It rained (cause), so the trail got muddy (effect).

notes.do: She reads each card out loud and covers it. Spend extra time on attempt and resolution: they are new words.
notes.say: Now we switch to reading. Every good story has a problem. Today, Theo's hike gets tricky.
notes.ask: What is the difference between a conflict and a resolution?
notes.listen: Conflict = the problem. Resolution = how it gets fixed at the end.

slides.title: The trail sign is missing
slides.text: Read this part out loud.

visual.text:
Theo’s First Hike (continued)
Near the top of the climb, the trail suddenly split into two paths, and the wooden sign that should have pointed the way was gone. Wind had knocked it over, and it lay half-buried in pine needles at Theo’s feet. His stomach tightened. To the left, the path curved into thick, shadowy trees. To the right, it opened onto bare rock. He had no idea which way led to Lookout Peak, and for a moment, he thought about turning around and heading back down.

items.q: Theo’s problem: the trail splits, and the ____ that should point the way is gone. Type one word.
items.why: The wooden sign is gone. Theo does not know which path to take.
items.no: Look at the first sentence. What should have pointed the way?

items.q: Which words show that Theo is worried?
choices: To the right, it opened onto bare rock.
Near the top of the climb
items.why: “His stomach tightened” is a body clue. It shows Theo feels worried.
no: That tells about the path, not about how Theo feels.
That tells where he is, not how he feels.

items.q: Why is this a conflict?
choices: The trees on the left path are shadowy and dark.
The path on the right opens onto bare rock.
He does not know which path is the right one.
items.why: A conflict is a problem the character must face. Theo must pick a path, and he does not know which one is right.
no: The trees are part of the setting. The problem is not knowing which way to go.
That tells about the path. The problem is not knowing which way to go.

notes.do: She reads aloud. Stop after "His stomach tightened" and ask how she would feel. Help with knocked, half-buried and shadowy if needed.
notes.ask: What is Theo's problem, in your own words? What does he think about doing?
notes.listen: "The sign is gone and he doesn't know which path goes to the peak." He thinks about turning around and going back down.

slides.title: Theo tries to solve it
slides.text: Read this part out loud.

visual.text:
Theo’s First Hike (continued)
Theo took a breath and thought about what to do. He could guess and hope he picked right. He could turn back and give up on seeing the valley. Or he could try something else. He remembered the old brass compass clipped to his belt, the one his father had given him that morning. He unclipped it, held it flat and steady in his palm, and watched the needle settle, pointing firmly north. Even the wind seemed to go still as he waited. Then he pulled out the folded trail map from his backpack and matched it against the compass. Lookout Peak, the map showed, was almost due north from where he stood.

items.q: Theo thinks of three choices: guess, turn back, or try something else. What tool does he unclip from his belt? Type one word.
items.why: Theo uses his compass. Then he matches it with his map.
items.no: He unclips something from his belt.
items.hint: It has a needle that points north.

items.q: Why is guessing a risky choice for Theo?
choices: He might pick the wrong path.
His father told him not to guess.
items.why: If Theo guesses, he might take the wrong path and not reach the peak.
no: Guessing is fast. The trouble is it could be wrong.
The story does not say that.

items.q: Who gave Theo the compass? Type one word.
items.why: The story says his father gave it to him that morning.
items.no: Look at the sentence about the old brass compass.

notes.do: She reads aloud. On the whiteboard, write Theo's three choices in a list. She puts a star by the one he picks.
notes.ask: Why is using the compass a better attempt than guessing or giving up?
notes.listen: Guessing could be wrong. Giving up means he never sees the valley. The compass and map help him find the right way. Theo uses a tool he got at the START of the story to solve a NEW problem.

slides.title: The resolution
slides.text: Read the last part out loud.

visual.text:
Theo’s First Hike (continued)
According to the compass, north pointed straight through the open rock path, not the shadowy trees. Theo clipped the compass back onto his belt, took one more breath, and turned right, toward the sunlight. Fifteen minutes later, the trees thinned out completely, and there it was: the whole valley, spread out below him just like his grandfather always said it would be, mist rising gold in the early sun. Theo grinned. He hadn’t just followed a trail today. He’d solved his first real problem, all on his own.

items.q: Which way does Theo turn? Type left or right.
items.why: Theo turns right, toward the sunlight and the open rock path.
items.no: The compass points through the open rock path. Which side was the rock on?

items.q: How does Theo feel at the end?
items.why: Theo grinned. He solved his first real problem all on his own. He feels proud and happy.
no: He found the way. He is not lost anymore.
He grinned. He is not bored or tired.

items.q: The resolution is how the problem gets ____. Type one word.
items.why: The resolution is how the problem gets fixed (or solved).
items.no: Think about the meaning card.
items.hint: It starts with f or s.

notes.do: She reads aloud. Ask her to show you Theo's grin.
notes.ask: What does Theo see at the top? Who told him about it?
notes.listen: The whole valley, just like his grandfather said. The ending connects back to Theo's goal from the first part of the story.

slides.title: Problem, try or fix?
slides.text: Tap a card. Then tap the box where it belongs.

items.text: The trail splits, and the sign is gone.
items.why: This is the problem Theo faces.
items.hint: Is this the problem, the try, or the fix?

items.text: Theo does not know which path is right.
items.why: Not knowing the way is the problem.

items.text: Theo holds the compass flat and watches the needle.
items.why: Using the compass is his try to fix the problem.

items.text: Theo matches the map to the compass.
items.why: This is part of his try.

items.text: Theo turns right and reaches the top.
items.why: He picked the right path. The problem is fixed.

items.text: Theo sees the whole valley and grins.
items.why: This is how the story ends. The problem is fixed.

slides.done: Problem, then try, then fix. That is the plot!

notes.do: She sorts. Then lay three index cards on the table: CONFLICT → ATTEMPT → RESOLUTION, with arrows between them.
notes.ask: Which card comes first in a story? Which comes last?
notes.listen: Conflict first, then attempt, then resolution.

slides.title: Cause and effect
slides.text: One thing causes the next. That links the plot together.

visual.text: conflict → attempt → resolution

steps.text: Cause: The sign is gone. → Effect: Theo does not know the way.
Cause: Theo does not know the way. → Effect: He uses his compass and map.
Cause: The compass shows north is the rock path. → Effect: He turns right.
Cause: He turns right. → Effect: He reaches the top and sees the valley.

notes.do: Point to the three index cards from the sort as you click each step.
notes.say: The cause comes first. The effect is what happens because of it.
notes.ask: Finish my sentence: The sign was gone, so …
notes.listen: "… Theo didn't know which way to go." Then: "Theo used the compass because …" → "he didn't know the way."

slides.title: Tell it in three parts
slides.text: Tell Theo’s plot out loud.
prompts: Tell one cause and effect. Use so.

notes.do: She retells with no help. Hold up the three index cards one at a time.
notes.listen: Three clear parts in order, using the words conflict, attempt and resolution. If she mixes up the order, point to the arrows on the cards.

slides.title: Words from memory
slides.text: No peeking at the word cards. Type the word.

items.q: A problem a character must face in a story is called a ____.
items.why: That is a conflict.
items.no: Theo’s missing sign is one.

items.q: A try at doing something hard is an ____.
items.why: That is an attempt.
items.no: Theo using his compass is one.

items.q: How the problem gets fixed at the end is the ____.
items.why: That is the resolution.
items.no: It is the last part of the plot.

items.q: Putting numbers from smallest to biggest is putting them in ____.
items.why: That is putting them in order.
items.no: It is a math word from today.

notes.do: No peeking. A missed word: she says it three times, spells it out loud, then types it again.
notes.listen: Spelling counts: c-o-n-f-l-i-c-t, a-t-t-e-m-p-t, r-e-s-o-l-u-t-i-o-n.

slides.title: Two big skills
slides.text: You compared numbers, and you found the whole plot.

steps.text: Compare: line up the places. Start at the left. Tie? Move right.
Symbols: the open side faces the bigger number.
Order: least to greatest means smallest first.
Plot: conflict → attempt → resolution.

slides.tip: Read the question. Does the bigger number win, or the smaller one?

notes.do: Give her the printed Packet. Open the course page together and read this week's task list, one day at a time.
notes.say: Tonight: the after-class lesson and Show What You Know. A little each day after that. Friday is Pathways Week 2 Reading. Monday is Pathways Week 2 Math.
notes.ask: Say the three compare steps without looking.
notes.listen: Line up the places, start at the left, tie means move right.

slides.title: On Your Own: Bigger or Smaller?
slides.text:
In class you compared numbers and found Theo’s problem.
Now you do it on your own.
Keep a pencil and paper close.

slides.title: Explain it out loud
slides.text: Say these to a grown-up, or say them out loud to yourself.
prompts: How do you compare two numbers? Where do you start?
What does < mean? What does > mean?
What was Theo’s conflict? What was the resolution?
starters: Theo’s problem was … In the end, …

slides.title: Line up, start left
slides.text: Compare 647 and 652.

steps.text: Hundreds: 6 and 6. A tie. Move right.
Tens: 4 and 5. 5 is more.
So 647 < 652. 647 is less than 652.

slides.tip: The open side faces the bigger number.

slides.title: Compare
slides.text: Line up the places on paper first.

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 8 is more than 3. So 283 > 238. 283 is greater than 238.
items.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 9 is more than 5. So 459 < 495. 459 is less than 495.
items.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 6 is more than 0. So 806 < 860. 806 is less than 860.
items.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.
items.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

items.q: Which one is true?
items.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 9 is more than 1. So 591 > 519.
no: Hundreds tie. Tens: 1 is less than 9. So 519 is smaller.
9 hundreds is more than 5 hundreds. 915 is bigger.
Same digits, different places. They are not equal.

slides.title: Least to greatest
slides.text: Tap the numbers from least to greatest.
slides.why: Hundreds first: 3 hundreds come before 5 hundreds. Then tens: 357 before 375, and 537 before 573.
slides.hint: Two numbers have 3 hundreds. Which of them has fewer tens?

slides.title: Order and race
slides.text: Read what wins before you answer.

items.q: Which is the greatest: 640, 604, 460? Type it.
items.why: Hundreds: 6, 6, 4. 640 and 604 tie. Tens: 4 is more than 0. 640 is greatest.
items.no: Two numbers have 6 hundreds. Compare their tens.

items.q: Ana swam in 205 seconds. Rob swam in 250 seconds. Who was faster?
items.why: 205 < 250. Ana’s time is smaller, so Ana was faster.
no: 250 is the bigger time. A bigger time is slower.
205 and 250 are not equal. The tens are different.

items.q: Put 481, 418, 841 in order from least to greatest. Type them with commas: ____
items.why: Hundreds: 4, 4, 8. 841 is last. 418 and 481 tie. Tens: 1 is less than 8. So: 418, 481, 841.
items.no: Least to greatest means smallest first.
items.hint: Two numbers have 4 hundreds. Which has fewer tens?

slides.title: Conflict, attempt, resolution
slides.text: Every story has a plot. The plot has three big parts.

visual.text: conflict → attempt → resolution

steps.text: Conflict: the problem.
Attempt: a try to fix it. Sometimes the first try does not work!
Resolution: how it gets fixed in the end.

slides.tip: Theo: the sign is gone → he uses the compass → he reaches the top.

slides.title: Tess’s Library Book
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text:
Tess’s Library Book
Tess’s library book was due today. She looked on her shelf. It was not there. Her heart thumped. She looked under her bed. She found only one old sock. Then Tess sat down and thought. “Where did I read it last?” she said. She remembered! She read it in the car. Tess ran outside and opened the car door. The book was under the seat. Tess smiled and hugged it. She took it back to the library just in time.

items.q: What is Tess’s conflict?
choices: She finds only one old sock under her bed.
Her book is due, and she cannot find it.
She does not want to read her library book.
items.why: Tess’s problem: the book is due today, and it is lost.
no: The sock is not her problem. What is she looking for?
The story never says that.

items.q: Tess’s first try does not work. Where does she look after the shelf? Type it.
items.why: She looks under her bed. She finds only a sock.
items.no: Read the sentence after “Her heart thumped.”

items.q: Where does Tess find the book? Under the car ____.
items.why: The book was under the seat in the car.
items.no: Read the part where she opens the car door.

items.q: Which words show Tess is worried?
items.why: “Her heart thumped” is a body clue. It shows she is worried.
no: Smiling shows she is happy, at the end.
That is what she does. It does not show a feeling.

slides.title: Sort Tess’s story
slides.text: Tap a card. Then tap the box where it belongs.

items.text: Tess cannot find her library book.
items.why: This is Tess’s problem.
items.hint: Is this the problem, the try, or the fix?

items.text: The book is due today.
items.why: This makes the problem big. She needs the book today.

items.text: Tess looks under her bed.
items.why: Looking is a try. This try does not work.

items.text: Tess sits and thinks: Where did I read it last?
items.why: Thinking back is another try. This one works!

items.text: Tess finds the book under the car seat.
items.why: The book is found. The problem is fixed.

items.text: Tess takes the book back just in time.
items.why: This is how the story ends.

slides.done: Problem, then try, then fix. You found the plot!

slides.title: Cause and effect
slides.text: A cause makes something happen. The effect is what happens.

items.q: Tess remembered she read the book in the car. What was the effect?
choices: She ran out to the car.
items.why: Because she remembered the car, she ran out to the car.
no: That happened before she remembered.
That happened before she remembered.

items.q: Theo’s sign was gone, so he did not know which ____ to take. Type one word.
items.why: The sign was gone (cause), so Theo did not know which path to take (effect).
items.no: Think about the fork in the trail.
items.hint: The trail split into two of these.

items.q: In cause and effect, what happens because of the cause is the ____.
items.why: What happens because of the cause is the effect.
items.no: Cause and ____.

slides.text: Place value, rounding and story words.

items.q: What is the 5 worth in 582?
items.why: The 5 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 500.
items.no: Find the place of the 5.

items.q: Round 73 to the nearest ten: ____
items.why: 73 is between 70 and 80. The ones digit is 3. Less than 5 rounds down: 70.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. Is it 5 or more?

items.q: Which is the expanded form of 805?
items.why: The 8 is worth 800, the 0 is worth 0, and the 5 is worth 5. 800 + 5 = 805.
no: 80 + 5 = 85. The 8 is in the hundreds place.
Those are just the digits. Use what each digit is worth.
800 + 50 = 850. The 5 is in the ones place.

items.q: A word that tells what a character is like (brave, shy, kind) is a ____.
items.why: That is a trait. Theo’s traits: brave and careful.
items.no: It is a story word from last lesson.

sets.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 4 is more than 3. So 734 < 743. 734 is less than 743.
sets.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.

sets.q: Which is the greatest: 385, 538, 358? Type it.
sets.why: Hundreds: 3, 5, 3. 5 is the biggest. 538 is greatest.

sets.q: Which list goes from least to greatest?
sets.why: 162 < 216 < 261 < 612. Smallest first.
no: 216 is bigger than 162. 1 hundred comes before 2 hundreds.
261 is bigger than 216. Hundreds tie, tens: 1 is less than 6.
That list goes from greatest to least.

sets.q: Kim biked the trail in 427 seconds. Lou biked it in 472 seconds. Who was faster?
sets.why: 427 < 472. Kim’s time is smaller, so Kim was faster.
no: 472 is the bigger time. A bigger time is slower.
427 and 472 are not equal. The tens are different.

sets.q: What is Ivy’s conflict? The lid on the jar is ____.
sets.why: Ivy’s problem: the lid is stuck, so she cannot get a pickle.

visual.text:
Ivy’s Stuck Jar
Ivy wanted a pickle. The lid on the jar was stuck. Ivy twisted and twisted. It would not open. Then she ran the lid under hot water. She twisted again. Pop! The lid came off. Ivy ate a big pickle.

sets.q: Which of Ivy’s attempts works?
choices: She twists the lid again and again.
She eats a big pickle at the end.
She runs hot water on the lid.
sets.why: The hot water works. Then the lid comes off. That fixes the problem.
no: She twists, but it will not open. That try does not work.
Eating the pickle is the end. It is not a try.

sets.q: Ivy runs hot water on the lid to open it. A try like that is called an ____.
sets.why: A try at doing something hard is an attempt.
sets.no: It means a try at doing something hard.

sets.q: How a story’s problem gets fixed at the end is the ____.
sets.why: That is the resolution.
sets.no: It is the last part of the plot.

sets.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.

sets.q: Which is the smallest: 196, 169, 619? Type it.
sets.why: Hundreds: 1, 1, 6. 196 and 169 tie. Tens: 6 is less than 9. 169 is smallest.
sets.no: Two numbers have 1 hundred. Compare their tens.

sets.q: Which one is true?
sets.why: Hundreds tie. Tens: 3 is less than 9. So 539 < 593.
no: 593 is the bigger one. Hundreds tie, tens: 9 is more than 3.
3 hundreds is less than 5 hundreds. 359 is smaller.
Same digits, different places. They are not equal.

sets.q: Which list goes from greatest to least?
sets.why: 970 > 907 > 790 > 709. Biggest first.
no: 970 is bigger than 907, so 970 goes first.
That list goes from least to greatest.
907 is bigger than 790. It must come before 790.

sets.q: What is Rosa’s conflict?
choices: Rain may get her cookies wet.
She does not have any cookies to sell.
Nobody wants to buy her cookies.
sets.why: Rosa’s problem: rain is falling on her cookie table.
no: She has a whole table of cookies.
People buy every one at the end.

visual.text:
Rosa’s Bake Sale
Rosa set up her cookie table outside. Then dark clouds rolled in. Big drops began to fall. “My cookies will get wet!” Rosa cried. She tried to cover them with a napkin. It was too small. So she carried her table under the library porch. People came to the dry porch to buy cookies. Rosa sold every one.

sets.q: Rosa’s first attempt does not work. What does she try to cover the cookies with? Type one word.
sets.why: She tries a napkin. It is too small.

sets.q: Rain falls (cause), so Rosa moves her table under the ____ (effect).
sets.why: She carries her table under the library porch, where it is dry.

sets.why: That is a conflict.

sets.no: Hundreds tie. Look at the tens.
sets.hint: The open side faces the bigger number.

sets.q: Which is the greatest: 719, 791, 197? Type it.
sets.why: Hundreds: 7, 7, 1. 719 and 791 tie. Tens: 9 is more than 1. 791 is greatest.
sets.no: Two numbers have 7 hundreds. Compare their tens.

sets.q: Four trails are 354, 345, 435 and 453 feet long. Which list goes from least to greatest?
sets.why: 345 < 354 < 435 < 453. Smallest first.
no: 345 is smaller than 354. It should come first.
That list goes from greatest to least.
435 is bigger than 354. 4 hundreds come after 3 hundreds.

sets.q: Max hiked for 316 minutes. Bea hiked for 361 minutes. Who took more time?
sets.why: 361 > 316. Bea’s time is bigger, so Bea took more time.
no: 316 is the smaller time. Max took less time.
316 and 361 are not equal. The tens are different.

sets.q: What is Kai’s conflict? His bike tire goes ____.
sets.why: Kai’s problem: his tire goes flat, so he cannot ride.

visual.text:
Kai’s Flat Tire
Kai rode his bike to the park. Halfway there, his tire went flat. Kai could not ride it. He pumped the tire up. Soon it went flat again. Kai walked his bike to his uncle’s shop. Uncle Ray put a patch on the tire. Kai rode to the park with a big grin.

sets.q: Kai pumps up the tire, and it goes flat again. What does this tell you?
choices: This part is the resolution of the story.
Kai’s first attempt does not work.
Kai gives up and walks home instead.
sets.why: Pumping the tire is a try. It does not work, so Kai has to try again.
no: The problem is not fixed yet. The tire goes flat again.
Kai does not give up. He walks to his uncle’s shop.

sets.q: What is the resolution? Uncle Ray puts a ____ on the tire.
sets.why: Uncle Ray puts a patch on the tire. Kai can ride again.
sets.no: Read the sentence about Uncle Ray.

pages.title: Part 5: Read and think
pages.directions:
Read the story. Then answer in full sentences.
Jay’s soccer ball rolled into the pond. It floated far from the edge. Jay tried to reach it with his foot. He almost fell in! Then he got a long stick. He pulled the ball close and grabbed it. Jay smiled and kicked it back to his team.

items.text: 14. What is Jay’s conflict?
15. What attempt does not work?
16. What is the resolution?
17. Finish the cause and effect: The ball rolled into the pond, so …

teacher.objective: Math (about 34 min): Ce'Line compares two 3-digit numbers by lining up the places and starting at the hundreds (a tie means move one place right), writes and reads the symbols <, > and = as "less than", "greater than" and "equal to", orders three or four numbers from least to greatest and greatest to least, and reads whether the bigger or the smaller number wins (race times, lightest pack). Reading (about 26 min, with the book talk): in Theo's First Hike (Pathways Week 2 Reading) she names the conflict, Theo's attempt and the resolution, links them with cause and effect, and types conflict, attempt and resolution from memory. A short warm-up reviews Week 1 (place value, rounding, setting).
materials: The class lesson on a laptop (teacher code 9110). She taps and types herself.
12 blank index cards and a pencil (number cards for comparing and ordering, then three cards: CONFLICT, ATTEMPT, RESOLUTION)
Small dry-erase board and 2 marker colors
Her printed Week 2 Packet (2 pages) to hand her at the end: page 1 Thursday, page 2 Saturday

plan.do: Class slides 1–2. What is the 4 worth in 452? Then she retells Theo's hike so far: who, where and when, what he wants. Make sure the compass from his father comes up.
Class slide 3. Value of the 7 in 374, round 46 and 350, setting. She types; you praise fast.
Class slide 4. Compare, greater than, less than, equal, order. She reads and covers each card.
Class slides 5–6. Index cards: 463 vs 389, 274 vs 281, 536 vs 532. She slides her finger left to right saying tie or wins.
Class slide 7. Whiteboard: 463 ___ 389. She draws the symbol and reads the sentence with greater than / less than.
Class slides 8–9. She says each sentence out loud before she types.
Class slides 10–11. She lines up 524, 342, 435 on cards, then 409, 490, 904, 940, then taps the order.
Class slide 12. She circles the key word (faster, lightest, greatest) before each answer.
Class slide 13 on her own: 693 ___ 639, smallest of 580/508/850, and the ordered list. Note her first answers.
Class slide 14. Conflict, solve, attempt, resolution, cause and effect.
Class slides 15–17. She reads each part aloud. Whiteboard list of Theo's three choices; she stars the one he picks.
Class slides 18–19. She sorts the six cards, then lays out CONFLICT → ATTEMPT → RESOLUTION index cards and finishes "The sign was gone, so …".
Class slide 20. She retells Theo's plot with the three words and one "so" sentence.
Class slide 21. Conflict, attempt, resolution, order typed with no peeking.
Class slide 22. Hand her the Packet. Open the course page and read this week's task list together.

watch: Starting at the wrong end: if she says 389 is bigger than 463 "because 8 and 9 are big," she is comparing digits, not places. Cover the tens and ones with a card and compare only the hundreds first.
Stopping at a tie: for 536 vs 532 she may say "they're the same" after the hundreds. Ask: did EVERY place tie? Slide to the right one place at a time.
Flipping the symbol: the open side faces the bigger number. Have her read every symbol as words ("is less than"); a symbol that reads wrong out loud is easy for her to catch.
Same digits, different places: 409/490/904/940 and 362/623 use the same digits. Point at each digit and ask what it is worth (Week 1 place value).
Least vs greatest: she circles least or greatest before ordering. Typed lists need commas or spaces between the numbers ("418, 481, 841").
Smaller wins: in races, a smaller time is faster. Before each word problem, she says out loud whether the bigger or the smaller number wins.

Conflict vs resolution: she may call the whole story "the problem." Use the three index cards: problem (conflict), try (attempt), fix (resolution). A first attempt can fail (Tess, Ivy, Rosa, Kai, Jay).
Confidence: she needs a lot of support and a lot of wins. Praise every correct step by name, read hard words with her, and let her answer out loud before she types.

packet_key.answer: Gia's time is smaller (258 < 285). In a race, the smaller time is faster.
Jay's soccer ball rolls into the pond, and it floats far from the edge.
He tries to reach it with his foot. (He almost falls in.)
He gets a long stick, pulls the ball close, grabs it, and kicks it back to his team.
Any true effect, for example: … so Jay had to find a way to get it back / so Jay tried to reach it with his foot.

She needs confidence first. Before class, check her Lesson 1 Show What You Know score and the Pathways Week 1 retakes from her task list; if place value is still shaky, spend 2 extra minutes on class slide 3 (what each digit is worth), because every compare uses it. Finish: if all three math exit-ticket items are right on the first try, she is ready for the Pathways Week 2 Math retake (Monday on her task list, aim for 85). She reads the whole Theo passage in class, so the Pathways Week 2 Reading retake (Friday) should feel familiar. Tonight she does the after-class lesson; it ends with Show What You Know (8 questions: 4 math and 4 reading; 3 different sets for retakes; she needs 7 of 8 for 85). If she scores under 85, look at the Formspree missed list: a missed compare or order means 10 minutes with index cards at the start of Lesson 3 (line up the places, start left, tie means move right); a missed race question means practicing "does the bigger or smaller number win?"; a missed plot question means retelling a short story with the three cards (conflict, attempt, resolution). She can retake the check during the week and gets a new set each time.
